content: The data reveals that 21% of blood donations were sourced from paid donors, while the type of donation for 15,965 apheresis platelet units remains unspecified. A geographical analysis of voluntary, non-remunerated blood donations (both whole blood and apheresis) by country is presented in Figure 8. In terms of apheresis donations, the total number and distribution by donation type are categorized by WHO regions. For example, the African Region (AFR) and the Region of the Americas (AMR) show varying proportions of voluntary, family/replacement, and paid donations. The Eastern Mediterranean Region (EMR) had the lowest proportion of female donors, with nine out of 12 countries reporting less than 10% of donations from women. However, countries like Egypt, Morocco, and Tunisia reported higher female donor contributions at 54%, 40%, and 35%, respectively. Globally, 30% of blood donations were from female donors, with significant regional and country-level variations. For instance, in the Eastern Mediterranean, the median proportion of female donors was only 7%, while in the Americas, it was 37%. Age-wise, 40% of donations came from donors aged 25–44 years, followed by 29% from those aged 45–64 years, and 23% from donors aged 18–24 years. Only 5% of donations were from individuals aged 65 years or older, and 3% were from those under 18 years. Younger donors contributed more in lowand middle-income countries compared to high-income countries, reflecting demographic differences. Repeat donors accounted for a significant proportion of voluntary, non-remunerated blood donations, with some European countries reporting 100% collection from repeat donors due to policies excluding first-time donors. The frequency of donations per donor per year varied, with some countries reporting potential underestimations due to database limitations. Regarding blood processing, 85% of whole blood donations globally were separated into components, with high-income countries achieving 97% processing rates compared to 50% in low-income countries. The South-East Asia and Eastern Mediterranean regions had the lowest processing rates at 61% and 65%, respectively. In contrast, over 90% of donations in the Americas, Europe, and the Western Pacific were processed into components. Laboratory screening policies for transfusion-transmissible infections (TTIs) such as HIV, hepatitis B (HBV), hepatitis C (HCV), and syphilis were reported by most countries. However, some countries faced challenges in achieving 100% screening due to irregular test kit supplies. For example, 35 countries reported stock-outs of test kits for TTIs. The prevalence of infection markers in blood donations is a critical indicator of blood safety.
